# Scientist Onsite: Experiment Design (Switchback + CI Interpretation)

[← Uber](../README.md) · [Every Uber question](../../uber.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/scientist-experiment-design)

`deep-dive` `math-reasoning` `ml-knowledge` `probability`

---

## Requirements

- Define the metric precisely. Marketplace measures are generally **ratios** (such as `rides / sessions`) rather than standalone counts, so make that clear in your opening sentence.
- Select the experimentation approach:
  - **A/B test** — suitable when assignment can be randomised per user without spillover.
  - **Switchback** — necessary when the treatment operates at the market level (city / time-of-day) and spillover makes user-level randomisation invalid. Changes to ETA, dispatch, or surge almost always call for switchback.
- Build the treatment buckets:
  - For treatments that vary continuously (for example, ETA multipliers of 0.8x / 1.0x / 1.2x), define the bucket grid and its guardrails.
  - Lay out rollout stages (1% → 10% → 50%) and identify the condition that causes a rollback.
- Read the results:
  - Apply 95% confidence intervals; for ratio measures, derive the CI with the delta method or bootstrap rather than using the ratio's standard error directly.
  - Address multiple-testing adjustments when several metrics were analysed.

## Notes

- The interviewer places particular emphasis on defining the metric quickly and accurately. Multiple candidates have failed after spending more than 5 minutes struggling with the definition; candidates with economics or data-science training tend to have an advantage.
- Candidates without an economics background should memorise the switchback decision tree ("if the treatment changes the marketplace → switchback; otherwise → A/B") to avoid using live interview time on that choice.
- Likely follow-up questions include:
  - "Why not use a straightforward A/B test?" — respond by explaining the spillover issue.
  - "How would you interpret an effect that appears at the 90% CI but not the 95% CI?" — cover statistical power, sample size, and multiple testing.
  - "Which guardrail metric would you choose?" — select one beforehand (for example, driver-side income or rider cancellations).
- Asking at the end of the round about the team's data infrastructure is reasonable.

- With switchback variance, **window length** is the main tuning parameter: windows that are too brief let carryover dominate (treated drivers continue reacting after the transition), while windows that are too long yield too few switches during the experiment. A commonly defensible starting point is 30–60-minute windows, with a 5-minute burn-in / burn-out period on both ends. Report CIs using bootstrap instead of an analytic SE for the ratio metric.

## Preparation

- Rehearse the switchback design pattern; several technical write-ups on switchback are relevant to this round.
- Practise calculating a ratio-metric CI by hand with the delta method.
- Prepare two ratio-metric experiment examples (one involving ETA and one involving a product surface) that you can readily use.
- Say a 60-second decision tree aloud: *Does the treatment affect a shared marketplace resource?* If so → switchback (city × time-of-day); if not → user-level A/B. Give this answer within the first 60 seconds to avoid getting stuck framing the problem.
